title: Observation of Universal Quantum Chaos at Shallow Depths
authors: Arman Sauliere, Guglielmo Lami, Hugo Lóio, Thomas J. Maldonado, Shashwat Kumar, Pedram Roushan, Andrea De Luca, Jacopo De Nardis
abstract: Universal statistical laws are a hallmark of quantum chaos, usually associated with the loss of spatial structure. Here we show, theoretically and experimentally, that universality emerges already at shallow depths in chaotic quantum circuits. We derive universal distributions of output-probability fluctuations and test them on a programmable superconducting processor. Two-dimensional lattices, open one-dimensional chains, and periodic rings exhibit distinct universality classes, retaining signatures of geometry and boundary topology before full random-matrix behavior emerges. Within each class, the distributions depend on only two parameters: an effective many-body Thouless length and the accumulated number of incoherent errors. Extracting these directly from measured bitstring frequencies provides access to scrambling, entanglement growth of the target state, and global fidelity, without reconstructing or classically simulating the implemented circuit. We also identify a noise-driven transition between output statistics retaining system-wide quantum correlations and those reproducible by independent small patches. Our results establish finite-depth universality as a practical tool for probing deep properties of quantum processors.
summary: This work establishes that universal quantum chaos statistics appear early in quantum circuits, even before full random matrix behavior is reached. By analyzing the Probability-of-Probabilities (PoP) distribution, the authors extract key metrics like scrambling and entanglement growth directly from measured output statistics. This provides a practical, finite-depth diagnostic tool for characterizing the deep quantum properties of superconducting processors.
main_problem: To demonstrate that universal statistical laws characteristic of quantum chaos emerge at shallow depths in quantum circuits, retaining signatures of the underlying geometry and boundary topology.
main_result: Universal Probability-of-Probabilities (PoP) distributions are established at finite depth, with distinct forms for different geometries (2D lattices, open/periodic chains), allowing access to scrambling and entanglement growth without full simulation.
method: The authors use theoretical derivations based on averaging over random circuit ensembles and relate the PoP moments to an effective classical statistical model involving permutations.
model_or_system: The study uses quantum circuits implemented on a programmable superconducting processor, modeling dynamics on 1D (open/periodic) and 2D lattices under random unitary evolution.
key_observables: Probability-of-Probabilities (PoP) distribution, PoP moments ($m_k$), effective many-body Thouless length ($\ell(t)$), and accumulated incoherent errors ($\eta(t)$).
important_parameters: Circuit depth ($t$), system size ($N$), and the ratio $\ell(t)/N$ which governs the transition between finite-depth and RMT regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the shallow-depth, weak-noise scaling limit for the transfer matrix expansion, and that ensemble averages are representative of typical circuit realizations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the replica statistical model, show PoP transitions based on depth and noise, and present count distributions for 1D circuits comparing measurements to theoretical fits for $\ell$ and $\eta$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical framework using replica methods to deriving distributions for specific geometries (1D/2D), extracting parameters ($\ell, \eta$) from measured statistics, and finally identifying noise-driven transitions.
why_interesting: The connection between measurable output statistics (PoP) and fundamental quantum information concepts like scrambling and entanglement growth, derived from statistical mechanics principles, provides a powerful, non-invasive diagnostic tool for quantum hardware.
